title: Maximum Pressure on Iran Will Fail
gist: A former NSC Iran director and 2025 Trump negotiating-team member argues that Trump's 2026 war and 'maximum pressure' blockade against Iran have failed: the war taught Tehran it can survive airstrikes, that the U.S. won't send ground troops, and that closing the Strait of Hormuz lets it impose reciprocal economic costs—so military and economic pressure have lost their utility and no future administration can revert to the 47-year playbook.

themes.theme: The failed war and its blowback

insights.claim: Trump launched a war against Iran in February 2026 aiming at regime change, but six months on faces a humiliation that threatens his party's midterm prospects, with the fallout impacting the U.S. mainly through higher gas prices.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Ties an ongoing Middle East war to U.S. domestic politics and energy prices—a live macro and midterm-election risk.
insights.locator: In February, when he launched his war

insights.claim: Trump's economic-pressure operation against Iran poses a greater threat to U.S. credibility than to Iran's economy as constructed.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Central contrarian claim that the flagship pressure campaign is net-negative for U.S. leverage—reframes how to read further escalation.
insights.quote: this economic-pressure operation poses a greater threat to U.S. credibility than it does to Iran’s economy

insights.claim: The war has so weakened Washington's ability to pressure Tehran that no future administration will be able to revert to the traditional 47-year U.S. playbook toward Iran.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Signals a durable structural break in U.S. Iran policy that outlasts Trump—relevant to long-run Gulf and oil-market risk.
insights.quote: no future administration will ever be able to revert to the traditional U.S. playbook
insights.locator: The irony of Trump’s failed war

themes.theme: Iran's dual nature as strategic constraint

insights.claim: Iran's regime is simultaneously ideological and transactional—retaining anti-American, anti-Israeli ideology while acting pragmatically, as when it accepted nuclear limits in 2015 and normalized ties with Saudi Arabia in 2023.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Explains why pure-pressure strategies misfire—any Iran forecast must price both ideological and transactional modes.
insights.quote: It is simultaneously ideological and transactional.

insights.claim: Kissinger's 2006 framing that Iran must decide 'whether they are representing a nation or a cause' reflected 50 years of U.S. policy that Tehran itself has never seen a need to resolve.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Identifies the flawed premise underlying U.S. strategy—Iran's refusal to choose is a feature, not a transitional phase.
insights.quote: decide whether they are representing a nation or a cause

insights.claim: In first-half-2025 negotiations Iranian negotiators focused less on sanctions relief than on securing nonaggression pledges from the United States and Israel.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: First-hand signal that security guarantees, not economics, are Tehran's priority—reshapes what any viable deal must contain.
insights.quote: Iranian negotiators were focused less on gaining sanctions relief than on securing nonaggression pledges from the United States and Israel
insights.locator: When I served on the Trump administration’s Iran negotiating team

themes.theme: Three lessons the war taught Tehran

insights.claim: Iran learned it can survive massive U.S. and Israeli airstrikes that killed its leaders and damaged infrastructure while keeping drone and missile capability intact enough to retaliate and halt Strait of Hormuz traffic.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Airstrikes strengthened rather than broke the regime, meaning further bombing is unlikely to change Tehran's calculus.
insights.locator: But this year’s war has taught the regime three new lessons

insights.claim: The war showed regime change in Iran requires a ground invasion that even the most hawkish U.S. policymakers won't publicly recommend, revealing Washington's limited ability to defeat Iran militarily.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Caps the credible U.S. military threat—Tehran now discounts it, reducing coercive leverage in any negotiation.
insights.quote: regime change cannot be accomplished in Iran without a ground invasion

insights.claim: Iran bet it could outlast the U.S. in a war of attrition because it will subject its people to more suffering than the U.S. public will bear, and Trump has repeatedly backed down when energy prices spiked.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Energy-price sensitivity is the pressure-release valve Tehran exploits—watch oil spikes as the trigger for U.S. de-escalation.
insights.quote: The Iranian regime is willing to subject its own people to more suffering and economic pain than the U.S. public is willing to bear

insights.claim: The threat of military force is now less valuable than before the war, which is why Trump's repeated military threats since the first cease-fire in April have not changed Tehran's actions.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Diminished threat credibility means saber-rattling headlines should be discounted as market-movers going forward.

insights.claim: Over 3,000 U.S. sanctions designations now target virtually every part of Iran's government and economy, but many are symbolic and became a default policy because they signal action while Americans rarely bear a direct cost.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Sanctions saturation means new designations carry little marginal bite—diminishing returns on the economic-pressure tool.
insights.quote: More than 3,000 U.S. sanctions designations now target virtually every aspect of Iran’s government and economy.

insights.claim: Trump escalated economic pressure to its zenith by blockading Iranian ports, but abandoned the first blockade after 66 days and has imposed a second he touts as the 'MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY.'
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: The 66-day retreat shows the blockade's own economic blowback caps its durability—a template for how the second one may unwind.
insights.quote: MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY
insights.locator: In the current war, Trump has cranked up

insights.claim: Iran's response to pressure is to use its missile and drone program to raise economic costs on the global economy—via the Strait of Hormuz or Gulf countries—shifting Trump's risk calculus rather than surrendering.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Each pressure escalation invites retaliation against Gulf energy infrastructure—a recurring tail risk for oil and shipping.

insights.claim: Trump degraded the value of sanctions relief by issuing oil-export waivers in March 2026 without Iranian concessions and again in June in return merely for a vow to keep the Strait of Hormuz open.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Giving away relief for nothing spends down the main future bargaining chip over Iran's nuclear program.
insights.locator: Whereas sanctions relief was once the reward

themes.theme: Successor strategies and the path forward

insights.claim: Potential Republican successors diverge sharply: Rubio favors expanding pressure and told Fox News the Iranian regime 'must change,' while Vance appears to favor retrenchment from Iran and the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: A Rubio-vs-Vance split defines the range of post-Trump Iran policy—key branching point for Gulf and energy exposure.

insights.claim: With newfound control of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has far more ability to make the United States and its Middle Eastern allies pay for applying pressure, undermining the strategy's core premise of low domestic cost.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: The pressure playbook only worked while it was cheap for Americans; Hormuz leverage removes that condition permanently.
insights.locator: A pressure strategy, however, was only sustainable

insights.claim: The author recommends Washington step back to force Iran's leadership to focus on governing rather than surviving a war, seek allied cooperation before unilateral action, and use accumulated leverage instead of building more.
insights.speaker: Nate Swanson
insights.so_what: Prescribes de-escalation and multilateralism—the policy signal to watch for if a reckoning actually reshapes U.S. strategy.
insights.locator: It is too early to know what path
